policy_title: Increase business taxes and clamp down on tax avoidance
stated: Increase the windfall tax on oil and gas production, close loopholes, introduce a windfall tax on banks with excessive profits, and make changes to VAT (reducing it on hospitality/arts, increasing on financial services/private education). Strengthen global tax agreements and HMRC resources to tackle tax dodging.

source.quote: Green MPs will support an increase in the rate of the windfall tax on oil and gas production and the closing of existing loopholes and tax-relief mechanisms. We would introduce a windfall tax on banks when excessive profits are being made. We would also propose a range of changes to VAT, reducing it on hard-pressed areas such as hospitality and the arts and increasing it on financial services and private education. It will be a priority to strengthen global tax agreements to stop corporate tax avoidance and evasion, and to ensure a level playing field between UK and transnational businesses. We will also ensure that HMRC has the resources it needs to reduce the gap between taxes due and taxes paid.

bearing_set.reason: VAT cuts on hospitality/arts directly reduce consumer prices in those sectors; VAT rises on financial services can feed through to banking/mortgage costs — both are non-negligible household cost-of-living effects.
Explicitly increases VAT on private education, raising school fees and potentially shifting pupils to the state sector — a direct, material effect on education access and state-school capacity.

The package — windfall taxes, loophole closure, private-education VAT rise, and expanded HMRC enforcement — is explicitly revenue-raising; it directly improves the funded/borrowed balance and the debt-sustainability path.

Targeting excess profits of oil/gas firms and banks, closing avoidance loopholes (disproportionately used by large firms and wealthy individuals), and shifting VAT toward private education and financial services narrows the income/wealth gap — a clear redistributive mechanism with a directional effect on inequality indicators.

Windfall taxes on oil/gas and banking, even if temporary, alter investment expectations in those sectors; the UK North Sea investment-disincentive debate is the canonical evidence of this mechanism, so the policy plausibly worsens business investment — a specific O13 indicator.

The explicit VAT changes directly affect household tax burden: the hospitality/arts VAT reduction lowers consumer prices for those spending in those sectors; the private-education and financial-services VAT increases raise the out-of-pocket cost for households using those services — a mixed but real and non-negligible distributional effect on what households keep.

membership_note: Four fundamentals earn real verdicts: O12 (primary revenue-raising purpose), O14 (redistribution from corporate profits/avoidance to public revenue), O13 (investment-disincentive mechanism in taxed sectors), and O11 (direct VAT changes on household spending). Effects on O2 (hospitality is not an essential) and O6 (oil-tax effect on extraction is too indirect) do not clear the non-negligible bar.
